title: Measures
hook: character traits are called middot, measures, meant to be set at the right amount

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: Mussar, the path of ethical self-work, trait by trait. Your line was work on a trait. Which trait did you pick for this block? Today, the Hebrew name for a trait. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-two.

A pinch of salt makes the bread. A cup of salt ruins it. Nobody in the kitchen calls salt good or bad. The only question anyone asks is how much. Turn up the heat and dinner cooks; turn it up too far and the smoke alarm goes off. Hebrew talks about a person's character the same way a cook talks about salt. The word for a trait, like patience or generosity or courage, is the word for a measure. Something you can have too little of, too much of, or just the right amount. That word is today's.
screen: `A PINCH MAKES THE BREAD.` → `A CUP RUINS IT.` → `A TRAIT IS A MEASURE.`

segments.voice: Middot. One trait is a middah, a measure; many traits are middot. Turn it four ways. First, the marketplace. In Leviticus, the Torah forbids cheating in judgment, in length, in weight, or in measure, and the Hebrew word there for the measure of length is middah. The same word that keeps a merchant's yardstick honest is the word Jewish teachers use for a person's character. A trait, in this language, is something you can check against a standard, the way you check a scale. Second, the middle. Maimonides, in his laws about character traits, describes each trait as stretching between two extremes. Take anger. At one end, the person who flares at everything. At the other, a person so numb nothing moves them, like the dead, he says. The way of the wise, he teaches, is usually the measure in between. Third, the exceptions. Maimonides did not make the middle a rule for everything. For pride and for anger, he advised going well past the middle, toward humility and calm, because those two do so much damage. So a measure is not always halfway; it is the right amount for that trait. Fourth, the highest use of the word. Jewish prayer calls the qualities God reveals to Moses in Exodus, merciful and gracious, slow to anger, the middot of mercy. The same word names God's ways and a person's habits. So when a Mussar teacher says work on your middot, the picture is not good traits versus bad ones. It is a set of dials. Too little patience, and you snap. Too much, and you let a wrong go on. Too little generosity, and your hand stays closed. Too much, and your own family goes without. The work is turning each dial toward its right setting, honestly, a little at a time.
screen: `THE SAME WORD KEEPS THE SCALE HONEST.` · `MOST TRAITS LIVE BETWEEN TWO ENDS.` · `PRIDE AND ANGER: GO PAST THE MIDDLE.` · `THE MIDDOT OF MERCY.` · then, large: `TRAITS ARE MEASURES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: measure one trait honestly. Settle, and breathe. Take the trait you chose yesterday, or any one that comes to mind. Picture a line in front of you. One end is too little of it. The other end is too much. Now place yourself on that line, as you were this past week. Not where you hope to be, and not where you fear you are. Just where the week puts you. Notice one moment that shows it. Then notice which way the dial might turn. You don't have to turn it yet. If you pray, you can bring this to God in your own words. If you don't, simply keep the picture of the line in view. The bell holds the time.
Middot. Measures: the Hebrew word for character traits, the same word the Torah uses for an honest measure in the market, each one meant to be set at its right amount. Today's word.
Your line: traits are measures. Today, when a trait shows up in you, sharp words or a soft yes, ask one quiet question: was that the right amount? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: In Mussar study groups, Jews often pick one middah, such as patience or generosity, study texts about it, and watch for it in their own week, aiming for its right measure rather than its extreme.

fork.setup: you're Maimonides, writing about anger. where do you set the right measure?
options: exactly halfway, like every other trait.
well past the middle, toward calm.
anywhere, as long as you mean well.
fork.reveal: for most traits he points to the middle, but for anger, and for pride, he advises going well past it, toward calm and humility.

original.note: Hebrew: measures. one trait is a middah, a measure.

trapdoor: what you thought: middot are the good traits a person should have.
what it means: measures. each trait can be too little, too much, or the right amount.
what a scholar hears: middah, the word in Leviticus for an honest measure, and the word prayer uses for God's middot of mercy.

notes: Leviticus 19:35: the lesson says the Hebrew word in the verse is middah (bammiddah, rendered 'meteyard' in older English). Confirm.
Hilchot De'ot 1:4 (the middle way, 'like the dead who feel nothing') and 2:3 (go to the far end for pride and anger) are paraphrased; confirm the paraphrase.
'Middot of mercy' for Exodus 34:6–7 follows liturgical usage; the count is deliberately left out.
